elements.element: Customer owns Deliverables and work product created for Customer.
elements.evidence: Retained 10.4: "Any writing or work of authorship created by M&I in the course of performing the Services under this Agreement, even if paid for by Customer, shall be the property of M&I ('Developed Software')" — ownership stays with Vendor; the redline deliberately targets the fallback instead.

elements.element: Vendor assigns the Deliverables and work product to Customer.
elements.evidence: No assignment language anywhere in the rendered text; 10.4 keeps title in M&I and even permits resale to other M&I customers.

elements.element: Vendor retains its pre-existing intellectual property.
elements.evidence: 10.4: "All programs (including ideas and know-how and concepts) developed by M&I are and shall remain M&I's sole property"; 17.2 confirms M&I systems remain M&I's.

elements.element: Customer's licence to Vendor IP embedded in Deliverables is perpetual.
elements.evidence: The new grant covers M&I-owned Developed Software rather than Vendor IP embedded in Customer-owned deliverables, and retained 17.2 limits Customer's rights in M&I-provided software to "use of the same during the Term", contradicting perpetuity.

elements.element: Customer's licence to embedded Vendor IP is irrevocable.
elements.evidence: Same defect: no Customer-owned deliverable exists and 17.2's "no rights ... except ... during the Term" survives unamended.

elements.element: Customer's licence to embedded Vendor IP is royalty-free.
elements.evidence: Royalty-free wording appears only in the new Developed Software grant; the preferred structure (Customer-owned deliverables containing licensed Vendor IP) is not created.

elements.element: Customer retains all rights in Customer Data.
elements.evidence: 17.1 retained: "Customer shall remain the sole and exclusive owner of all Customer Data and other Confidential Information."

elements.element: Any Vendor licence in Customer Data is limited to processing it solely to provide the Services.
elements.evidence: Insertion into 17.1 reads "M&I may process Customer Data solely to provide the Services and for no other purpose", but the drafter's own rationale identifies 17.4 as permitting use for the broader "purposes contemplated by this Agreement" and 17.4 was not edited or overridden — a surviving broader use right defeats this element.

elements.element: The parties do not jointly own intellectual property.
elements.evidence: No joint-ownership language appears in 10.4, 17.1 or 17.2; ownership is allocated unilaterally in each clause.

elements.element: Vendor may retain ownership of generic tools and know-how.
elements.evidence: Retained 10.4: "All programs (including ideas and know-how and concepts) developed by M&I are and shall remain M&I's sole property."

elements.element: Customer's licence to Deliverables is perpetual.
elements.evidence: New sentence says "perpetual", but retained 17.2 ("Customer acknowledges that it has no rights in any software, systems, documentation ... provided by M&I, except with respect to Customer's use of the same during the Term") is left unamended and expressly contradicts a post-Term right in Developed Software; the grant is internally inconsistent.

elements.element: Customer's licence to Deliverables is irrevocable.
elements.evidence: Same conflict: 17.2's Term-limited "no rights" acknowledgement survives, so irrevocability is contradicted by retained language rather than cleanly granted.

elements.element: Customer's licence to Deliverables is worldwide.
elements.evidence: "M&I grants Customer a perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free license ..." — no retained geographic restriction conflicts.

elements.element: Customer's licence to Deliverables is royalty-free.
elements.evidence: Express "royalty-free" in the inserted licence; the 10.4 refund/credit mechanic is a Customer benefit and does not impose a royalty.

elements.element: Customer may use and modify Deliverables for its business.
elements.evidence: "license to use, modify and sublicense the Developed Software for Customer's business" — use and modification rights are express (though 17.2's "use ... during the Term" wording should still be conformed).

elements.element: Customer may sublicense Deliverables for its business.
elements.evidence: "use, modify and sublicense the Developed Software for Customer's business"; the Article 23 sublicense bar applies to the source-code licence, not to this new Developed Software grant, but see reasons for a conforming carve-out.

elements.element: Any Vendor licence in Customer Data is limited to processing it solely to provide the Services.
elements.evidence: The 17.1 insertion is correctly worded, but the broader 17.4 permission to use Customer Data for the "purposes contemplated by this Agreement" (identified in the finding's own rationale) was not struck or overridden, leaving a contradictory retained grant.

reasons: Fallback is incomplete: the perpetual and irrevocable limbs of the new Developed Software licence are contradicted by retained 17.2 ("no rights in any software ... provided by M&I, except with respect to Customer's use of the same during the Term"). Repair by amending 17.2 to read "except with respect to Customer's use of the same during the Term and except as expressly licensed to Customer under Section 10.4" (or open the new licence with "Notwithstanding Section 17.2").

Fallback element 8 is not met in operative language: the limiting sentence was inserted in 17.1 while the broader use permission in 17.4 ("purposes contemplated by this Agreement") remains untouched. Repair by editing 17.4 itself to "solely to provide the Services" or by adding "Notwithstanding Section 17.4" to the 17.1 insertion; the rationale claims 17.4 was narrowed, but no operation reaches it.

Preferred level is not attempted and fails on ownership/assignment (10.4 keeps title to paid-for work of authorship in M&I and permits resale to other customers); targeting the fallback is a defensible choice, but the finding should not be treated as position-complete.

Minimality is satisfied: the two insertions are concise, nothing favourable was deleted, and no extras (survival tails, expense or damages language, procedures) were added. The only surplus is the redundant "and for no other purpose" after "solely" — harmless but strikeable.

Intent is not preserved because two retained sentences (17.2's Term-limited "no rights" acknowledgement and 17.4's broader Customer Data use permission) now contradict the inserted operative terms; fix both before sending.

Also consider a conforming reference so the Article 23 source-code licence ("through the end of the Term", no sublicensing) is expressed as without prejudice to the new Section 10.4 licence, avoiding an argument that the narrower Article 23 terms govern Developed Software.
